intro: The graph point is the one lost most often on the AP® Macroeconomics exam. Graph Studio has the eight graph kinds the course draws (nine graphs, since the short- and long-run Phillips curves share one): pick a graph, pick what happens, and shift the curve yourself. Test yourself grades every graph point by point, the way readers score it: the labels, the right curve shifted the right way, the new equilibrium, and what it means.
howItWorks:
Explore. Choose a graph, then choose what happens. Drag the curve you think moves (or use its button and the arrow keys); the new equilibrium E2 follows where the curves cross. Show me draws the shift for you, and Why walks through the cause, the curve, the direction and the result. Details lists what shifts each curve.

Test yourself. Each problem is one graph, built one rubric point at a time: label the axes and curves, shift the right curve, move E2, then read the result. A slip is named the way a reader would see it, such as shifting aggregate demand when the change shifts short-run aggregate supply. Your first try at each step is what counts toward mastery.

Magnitude is never graded: only which curve moves, which way, and where E2 sits against E1.

The PPC and supply-and-demand drills are free. The other graphs' drills are part of Premium; Explore is open for every graph.

settings.adas: An economy starts at its short-run equilibrium.
settings.reserves: The market for bank reserves, with ample reserves.
settings.phillips: An economy starts at long-run equilibrium on its Phillips curves.

graphs.title: Production possibilities curve
graphs.shows: Every combination of two goods an economy can make with all its resources and today's technology.
graphs.axes: Each axis is one of the two goods, by name. The curve is bowed out because resources are not equally good at making both goods, so the opportunity cost rises.

list: Out: more or better resources (labor, capital, land), more human capital, better technology
In: resources lost (a disaster, a war), technology lost

graphs.movement: Moving resources from one good to the other is a movement along the curve: the opportunity cost is the other good given up. A point inside means unemployed or wasted resources; a point outside cannot be reached now.

graphs.title: Supply and demand
graphs.shows: One market: how much buyers want and sellers offer at each price, and where they agree.
graphs.axes: Price on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal. Never Price level or Real GDP: those belong to the whole economy.
graphs.movement: A change in the good's own price is a movement along both curves (a change in quantity demanded and quantity supplied), never a shift.

graphs.title: Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
graphs.shows: The whole economy: total spending (AD), what firms produce in the short run (SRAS) and full-employment output (LRAS).
graphs.axes: Price level on the vertical axis, Real GDP (real output) on the horizontal. LRAS is vertical at full-employment output.

list: Net exports: foreign incomes, exchange rates
Quantity and quality of labor and capital

graphs.movement: A change in the price level is a movement along AD and SRAS (the wealth, interest rate and exchange rate effects), never a shift.
graphs.link: Beside it, the Phillips curves: an AD shift is a movement along the short-run Phillips curve, an SRAS shift moves it the other way.

graphs.title: Money market
graphs.shows: How much money people want to hold (MD) against the money supply the central bank sets (MS), which sets the nominal interest rate.
graphs.axes: Nominal interest rate on the vertical axis (never real), Quantity of money on the horizontal. MS is vertical.

list: Limited reserves: open market operations (buy bonds: right; sell: left)

graphs.movement: A change in the nominal interest rate is a movement along money demand. With ample reserves the Federal Reserve sets rates with administered rates; see the reserve market.

graphs.title: Market for bank reserves
graphs.shows: Ample reserves, the framework the Federal Reserve uses now: reserve demand is flat at the administered rate, and reserve supply crosses it in the flat part.
graphs.axes: Policy interest rate (the federal funds rate) on the vertical axis, Quantity of reserves on the horizontal. Reserve supply is vertical.

list: The administered rates: interest on reserve balances and the overnight reverse repurchase rate move the flat part up or down
Central bank purchases (right) or sales (left) of securities

graphs.movement: With ample reserves, shifting reserve supply along the flat part leaves the policy rate alone: the rate moves when the administered rates do.

graphs.title: Loanable funds market
graphs.shows: Saving supplied to borrowers (SLF) and borrowing for investment and deficits (DLF), which set the real interest rate.
graphs.axes: Real interest rate on the vertical axis (never nominal), Quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal.

list: Investment demand: expected profits, investment tax credits
Government borrowing to finance a deficit
Foreign capital flowing in (right) or out (left)

graphs.movement: A change in the real interest rate is a movement along both curves. Higher government borrowing raises the real interest rate and crowds out private investment.

graphs.title: Short-run and long-run Phillips curves
graphs.shows: The short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment (SRPC) and the natural rate of unemployment (LRPC).
graphs.axes: Inflation rate on the vertical axis, Unemployment rate on the horizontal. LRPC is vertical at the natural rate; SRPC meets it at the expected inflation rate.

list: Expected inflation (higher: up and to the right)
Supply shocks: SRAS left moves SRPC right
The natural rate of unemployment: frictional and structural unemployment
What shifts LRAS shifts LRPC the other way

graphs.movement: An AD shift is a movement along the short-run Phillips curve: more spending, lower unemployment, higher inflation.
graphs.link: Beside it, AD-AS: the same shock seen as output and the price level.

graphs.title: Foreign exchange market
graphs.shows: The market for one currency: foreigners demand it to buy the country's goods and assets, and its own residents supply it to buy foreign ones.
graphs.axes: Price of the currency in the other currency per unit of this one (nells per garv in the market for garvs), and Quantity of the currency. The ratio upside down loses the point.

list: Foreign demand for the country's exports (foreign incomes, tastes)
Relative real interest rates: higher here pulls financial capital in
The country's demand for imports (its own incomes, tastes)
Its residents buying foreign assets (higher rates abroad)

graphs.movement: Appreciation is a rise in the currency's price; it makes exports dearer abroad, so net exports fall.
graphs.link: Beside it, the mirror market for the other currency: demand for one is supply of the other.

scenarios.title: Better technology
scenarios.cause: A new technology raises productivity in making both {x} and {y}.
why: With better technology the same resources make more of both goods, so every point on the curve moves out.
That is economic growth: combinations that were out of reach become possible.

scenarios.title: A larger labor force
scenarios.cause: Many more workers join the labor force.
why: More labor is more resources, so the economy can make more of both goods.
The curve shifts out; moving along it would only trade one good for the other.

scenarios.title: More capital
scenarios.cause: Years of investment build up a larger stock of machines and buildings.
why: Capital is a resource, so a larger capital stock lets the economy make more of both goods.
This is why an economy that makes more capital goods today can grow faster later.

scenarios.title: A natural disaster
scenarios.cause: A flood destroys a large share of the country's factories and farmland.
scenarios.because: the loss of capital and land
why: Destroyed factories and farmland are lost resources, so the economy can make less of both goods.
The whole curve shifts in. A recession with idle resources would be a point inside the curve instead.

scenarios.title: Workers left unemployed
scenarios.cause: A recession leaves many workers unemployed and factories idle.
scenarios.ask: the combination the economy makes during the recession.
scenarios.pointWhy: inside the curve, because unemployed workers and idle factories are resources not being used.
why: Unemployment does not destroy resources, so the curve itself stays put; the economy just produces inside it.
Putting the idle resources back to work moves the economy toward the curve without giving up either good.

scenarios.title: Every resource used efficiently
scenarios.cause: Every worker and machine is employed, and each is used where it is most productive.
scenarios.pointWhy: on the curve, because full and efficient use of resources is exactly what the curve shows.
why: On the curve, more of one good means giving up some of the other: that is opportunity cost.

scenarios.title: More than the economy can make
scenarios.cause: Planners ask for more of both goods than the economy can make with today's resources and technology.
scenarios.ask: the combination the planners ask for.
scenarios.pointWhy: outside the curve, because no use of today's resources and technology reaches it.
why: A point outside the curve becomes reachable only if the curve shifts out: more resources or better technology.

scenarios.title: Incomes rise (a normal good)
scenarios.cause: Incomes rise, and buyers treat {good} as a normal good.
scenarios.because: higher incomes for a normal good

slips.S: Incomes belong to buyers, so they change demand, not supply. Sellers' costs have not changed.

why: Income is a demand shifter: with more income, buyers want more of a normal good at every price.
Demand shifts right, so at the old price there is a shortage; the price rises until the market clears at a higher price and quantity.

scenarios.title: A substitute gets dearer
scenarios.cause: The price of {sub}, a substitute for {good}, rises.
scenarios.because: a higher price of a substitute

slips.S: A substitute's price changes what buyers choose, so it shifts demand. Producers of this good face the same costs.

why: When a substitute gets dearer, some buyers switch to this good, so demand shifts right.
The new equilibrium has a higher price and a higher quantity.

scenarios.title: A complement gets dearer
scenarios.cause: The price of {comp}, which buyers use with {good}, rises.
scenarios.because: a higher price of a complement

slips.S: A complement's price changes how much buyers want this good, so it shifts demand, not supply.

why: Goods used together are complements: when one gets dearer, buyers want less of both.
Demand shifts left: the price and the quantity both fall.

scenarios.title: Tastes turn against it
scenarios.cause: A widely shared report convinces many buyers that {good} is bad for them.
why: Tastes and preferences are a demand shifter: buyers want less at every price.
Demand shifts left, so the price and the quantity fall.

scenarios.title: Buyers expect a higher price
scenarios.cause: Buyers expect the price of {good} to rise next month, so they buy more now.
scenarios.because: buyers expecting a higher future price
why: Expecting a higher price later, buyers bring purchases forward: demand today shifts right.
Today's price and quantity both rise.

scenarios.title: More buyers
scenarios.cause: The town's population grows quickly, bringing many new buyers of {good}.
why: More buyers means more quantity demanded at every price: demand shifts right.
The price and the quantity rise.

scenarios.title: An input gets dearer
scenarios.cause: The price of {input}, an input used to make {good}, rises.
scenarios.because: a rise in the price of {input}

slips.D: An input price changes what it costs to make the good, so it shifts supply. Buyers did not change what they want.

why: A higher input price raises the cost of producing each unit, so sellers offer less at every price: supply shifts left.
At the old price there is a shortage; the price rises and the quantity falls.

scenarios.title: A cheaper way to make it
scenarios.cause: A new machine lets producers make {good} at a lower cost per unit.

slips.D: Technology changes the cost of producing, so it shifts supply. Buyers want the same amount at each price.

why: Lower costs mean sellers offer more at every price: supply shifts right.
The price falls and the quantity rises.

scenarios.title: A per-unit tax on sellers
scenarios.cause: The government puts a tax on producers for every unit of {good} they sell.

slips.D: A tax on producers raises their cost of selling each unit, so it shifts supply, not demand.

why: The tax works like a higher cost per unit: supply shifts left.
The price buyers pay rises and the quantity falls.

scenarios.title: A per-unit subsidy
scenarios.cause: The government pays producers a subsidy for every unit of {good} they make.
why: A subsidy lowers producers' cost per unit: supply shifts right.
The price falls and the quantity rises.

scenarios.title: More sellers
scenarios.cause: Many new firms start producing {good}.
why: More sellers offer more at every price: supply shifts right.
The price falls and the quantity rises.

scenarios.title: The price rises; buyers buy less
scenarios.cause: The price of {good} rises, and buyers choose to buy less.
why: The good's own price is on the vertical axis, so a change in it moves buyers along the demand curve: a change in quantity demanded, not in demand.

scenarios.title: The price rises; sellers offer more
scenarios.cause: The price of {good} rises, and producers offer more for sale.
why: The good's own price is on the vertical axis, so a change in it moves sellers along the supply curve: a change in quantity supplied, not in supply.

scenarios.title: Consumer confidence rises
scenarios.cause: Households grow more confident about their jobs and spend more of their income.

slips.SRAS: Consumer spending is part of aggregate demand (C + I + G + Xn), so it shifts AD. Firms' costs have not changed.

why: Consumption is a component of AD, so more consumer spending shifts AD right.
Along SRAS, real output and the price level both rise, and unemployment falls.

scenarios.title: Government spending rises
scenarios.cause: The government raises its spending on roads and schools.

slips.SRAS: Government purchases are part of aggregate demand, so they shift AD, not SRAS.
slips.LRAS: In the short run, new government purchases are spending: they shift AD. LRAS moves only when the economy's resources or technology change.

why: Government spending is a component of AD: AD shifts right (by more than the spending, through the multiplier).
Real output and the price level rise.

scenarios.title: Income taxes rise
scenarios.cause: The government raises personal income taxes.

slips.SRAS: Personal income taxes cut households' disposable income, so consumption and AD fall. They do not change firms' costs.

why: Higher taxes leave households less disposable income, so consumption falls and AD shifts left.
Real output and the price level fall, and unemployment rises.

scenarios.title: Trading partners grow richer
scenarios.cause: Incomes rise in the country's trading partners, so they buy more of its exports.
why: Exports are part of net exports, a component of AD: AD shifts right.
Real output and the price level rise.

scenarios.title: Firms turn pessimistic
scenarios.cause: Firms expect weaker sales and cut their spending on new equipment.

slips.SRAS: Spending on new equipment is investment, a component of AD, so AD shifts. Production costs have not changed.

why: Investment is a component of AD: lower investment shifts AD left.
Real output and the price level fall, and unemployment rises.

scenarios.title: Household wealth falls
scenarios.cause: Stock and home prices fall sharply, so households feel poorer and spend less.
why: Less wealth means less consumption at every price level: AD shifts left.
Real output and the price level fall.

scenarios.title: Oil prices jump
scenarios.cause: The price of oil, an input used across the economy, rises sharply.

slips.AD: Input costs change what firms can supply at each price level, so they shift SRAS, not AD.
slips.LRAS: A rise in input prices is a short-run supply shock: it shifts SRAS. LRAS depends on the economy's resources and technology.

why: Higher input costs mean firms supply less real output at every price level: SRAS shifts left.
The price level rises while real output falls: stagflation, with higher unemployment.

scenarios.title: Nominal wages rise
scenarios.cause: Nominal wages rise across the economy while productivity stays the same.

slips.AD: Wages are firms' biggest cost, so higher nominal wages shift SRAS left. In this model the wage change works through costs, not spending.

why: Higher nominal wages raise production costs: SRAS shifts left.
The price level rises and real output falls.

scenarios.title: Energy gets cheaper
scenarios.cause: The price of energy falls across the economy.

slips.AD: Energy is an input, so cheaper energy lowers costs and shifts SRAS, not AD.

why: Lower input costs mean firms supply more at every price level: SRAS shifts right.
The price level falls and real output rises.

scenarios.title: More resources (long run)
scenarios.cause: The labor force grows and firms add to the capital stock.
why: More labor and capital raise full-employment output: LRAS shifts right, and SRAS usually shifts right with it.
With AD unchanged, real output rises and the price level falls. This is long-run economic growth.

scenarios.title: The price level rises; spending falls
scenarios.cause: The price level rises, so households, firms and foreigners buy less real output.
why: The price level is on the vertical axis, so its change is a movement along AD: the wealth, interest rate and exchange rate effects.

scenarios.title: The price level rises; firms produce more
scenarios.cause: The price level rises while nominal wages are fixed for now, so firms produce more real output.
why: The price level is on the vertical axis, so firms move along SRAS: with wages sticky in the short run, higher prices make more output profitable.

scenarios.title: Limited reserves: buy bonds
scenarios.cause: With limited reserves, the central bank buys government bonds on the open market.
scenarios.because: an open market purchase of bonds

slips.MD: Buying bonds pays banks new reserves, which expand the money supply: MS shifts, not money demand.

why: Paying for the bonds adds reserves to banks, which lend them out: the money supply shifts right.
The nominal interest rate falls, which raises investment and interest-sensitive consumption, so AD rises.

scenarios.title: Limited reserves: sell bonds
scenarios.cause: With limited reserves, the central bank sells government bonds on the open market.
scenarios.because: an open market sale of bonds

slips.MD: Selling bonds drains reserves from banks, which shrinks the money supply: MS shifts left, not money demand.

why: Buyers pay for the bonds out of bank deposits, so reserves and the money supply fall: MS shifts left.
The nominal interest rate rises, so investment and AD fall.

scenarios.title: Limited reserves: lower the reserve requirement
scenarios.cause: With limited reserves, the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio.
why: A lower required reserve ratio turns some required reserves into excess reserves that banks can lend, and raises the money multiplier: MS shifts right.
The nominal interest rate falls.

scenarios.title: Limited reserves: raise the discount rate
scenarios.cause: With limited reserves, the central bank raises the discount rate.
why: Borrowing reserves from the central bank costs more, so banks borrow fewer reserves and lend less: MS shifts left.
The nominal interest rate rises.

scenarios.title: Real GDP rises
scenarios.cause: Real GDP rises, so people make more purchases and want to hold more money for them.

slips.MS: The central bank sets the money supply; a change in income changes how much money people want to hold, which is money demand.

why: More transactions mean people want to hold more money at every interest rate: MD shifts right.
With MS vertical, the quantity of money stays the same and the nominal interest rate rises.

scenarios.title: The price level rises
scenarios.cause: The price level rises, so every purchase takes more money.

slips.MS: A higher price level changes how much money people need, which is money demand; the central bank has not changed the money supply.

why: At higher prices people need more money for the same purchases: MD shifts right.
The nominal interest rate rises, and bond prices fall (they move opposite to interest rates).

scenarios.title: The price level falls
scenarios.cause: The price level falls, so each purchase takes less money.
why: At lower prices people need less money for their purchases: MD shifts left.
The nominal interest rate falls.

scenarios.title: Lower the administered rates
scenarios.cause: With ample reserves, the central bank lowers the interest rate it pays on reserve balances and its other administered rates.

slips.RS: With ample reserves, adding reserves on the flat part leaves the policy rate alone. The central bank lowers the rate by lowering its administered rates, which moves the flat part of reserve demand down.

why: Banks will not lend reserves for less than they earn holding them, so the administered rates set the flat part of reserve demand. Lowering them shifts it down.
The policy rate falls, other interest rates follow, and investment and AD rise.

scenarios.title: Raise the administered rates
scenarios.cause: With ample reserves, the central bank raises the interest rate it pays on reserve balances and its other administered rates.

slips.RS: With ample reserves, draining some reserves on the flat part does not raise the policy rate. Raising the administered rates moves the flat part of reserve demand up.

why: Raising the rate paid on reserves raises the flat part of reserve demand: it shifts up.
The policy rate rises, other interest rates follow, and investment and AD fall.

scenarios.title: Buy securities, reserves stay ample
scenarios.cause: With ample reserves, the central bank buys securities, adding reserves; reserves stay in the ample range.

slips.RD: Buying securities changes the quantity of reserves, which is reserve supply. Reserve demand moves only with the administered rates.

why: Paying for the securities adds reserves: reserve supply shifts right.
It crosses reserve demand on the flat part, so the policy rate stays the same. That is why, with ample reserves, the rate is set with administered rates.

scenarios.title: Sell securities, reserves stay ample
scenarios.cause: With ample reserves, the central bank sells securities, draining some reserves; reserves stay in the ample range.
why: Selling securities drains reserves: reserve supply shifts left.
Still on the flat part, the policy rate stays the same.

scenarios.title: A larger budget deficit
scenarios.cause: The government runs a larger budget deficit and borrows to cover it.
why: The government borrows in the loanable funds market: the demand for loanable funds shifts right. (Drawing it as less public saving, the supply of loanable funds shifting left, is also scored right.)
The real interest rate rises, so private investment falls: crowding out, which slows the growth of the capital stock.

scenarios.title: Households save more
scenarios.cause: Households decide to save a larger share of their income.

slips.DLF: Saving is the source of loanable funds, so more saving shifts supply. Borrowers have not changed what they want.

why: Saving is the supply of loanable funds: it shifts right.
The real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds rises, so investment rises.

scenarios.title: Households save less
scenarios.cause: Households spend more and save a smaller share of their income.
why: Less saving shifts the supply of loanable funds left.
The real interest rate rises and the quantity of loanable funds falls.

scenarios.title: Firms want to invest more
scenarios.cause: Firms expect high profits from new equipment and want to borrow more to buy it.

slips.SLF: Firms borrowing to invest are on the demand side of loanable funds, so DLF shifts.

why: Borrowing to invest is the demand for loanable funds: it shifts right.
The real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds rise.

scenarios.title: Foreign savers move funds in
scenarios.cause: Foreign savers move funds into the country's bonds and bank accounts.

slips.DLF: Foreign funds coming in are more saving to lend, so they shift the supply of loanable funds.

why: Funds flowing in from abroad add to the saving available to borrowers: SLF shifts right.
The real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds rises.

scenarios.title: Savers send funds abroad
scenarios.cause: Domestic savers move funds abroad to earn higher returns there.
why: Funds leaving the country reduce the saving available to borrowers: SLF shifts left.
The real interest rate rises.

scenarios.title: AD rises (demand-pull)
scenarios.cause: Aggregate demand rises.
scenarios.ask: where the economy moves in the short run.
scenarios.pointWhy: up and to the left along the short-run Phillips curve: lower unemployment and higher inflation.
why: An AD shift is a movement along SRPC, not a shift of it: more spending raises output (unemployment falls) and the price level (inflation rises).
In the long run, expected inflation rises and SRPC shifts up until unemployment is back at the natural rate.

scenarios.title: AD falls
scenarios.cause: Aggregate demand falls.
scenarios.ask: where the economy moves in the short run.
scenarios.pointWhy: down and to the right along the short-run Phillips curve: higher unemployment and lower inflation.
why: An AD shift is a movement along SRPC: less spending lowers output (unemployment rises) and inflation falls.

scenarios.title: Expected inflation rises
scenarios.cause: Workers and firms come to expect higher inflation and build it into wages and prices.

slips.LRPC: Expected inflation moves the short-run curve. LRPC sits at the natural rate of unemployment, which expectations do not change.

why: Higher expected inflation shifts SRPC up (to the right): every unemployment rate now comes with more inflation.
The new long-run point, where SRPC meets LRPC, has the same natural rate of unemployment and a higher inflation rate.

scenarios.title: Expected inflation falls
scenarios.cause: Workers and firms come to expect lower inflation.
why: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down (to the left).
At the new long-run point, unemployment is at the natural rate and inflation is lower.

scenarios.title: A negative supply shock
scenarios.cause: Oil prices jump, so SRAS shifts left.

slips.LRPC: A supply shock is a short-run change: it shifts SRPC. LRPC moves only when the natural rate of unemployment changes.

why: SRAS left raises the price level and lowers output, so inflation and unemployment both rise: SRPC shifts right.
That is stagflation. LRPC stays at the natural rate.

scenarios.title: The natural rate falls
scenarios.cause: Better job-matching services cut frictional unemployment, so the natural rate of unemployment falls.
scenarios.because: a lower natural rate of unemployment

slips.SRPC: The natural rate of unemployment is where LRPC stands, so a lower natural rate shifts LRPC left.

why: LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, so it shifts left.
On AD-AS the same change is LRAS shifting right.

scenarios.title: Foreigners buy more exports
scenarios.cause: Residents of {abroad} buy more goods made in {home}.

slips.S: Buyers in {abroad} need {cur}s to pay for {home}'s goods, so they demand {cur}s. Supply of the {cur} comes from {home}'s own residents.

why: To pay for {home}'s goods, buyers in {abroad} trade {other}s for {cur}s: the demand for the {cur} shifts right.
The {cur} appreciates (it costs more {other}s), which makes {home}'s exports dearer and its imports cheaper, so its net exports fall from there.

scenarios.title: Fewer foreign tourists
scenarios.cause: Fewer tourists from {abroad} visit {home}.

slips.S: Tourists from {abroad} buy {cur}s to spend in {home}, so fewer tourists means less demand for the {cur}.

why: Tourists buy {cur}s to spend in {home}: the demand for the {cur} shifts left.
The {cur} depreciates.

scenarios.title: Real interest rates rise here
scenarios.cause: Real interest rates in {home} rise relative to {abroad}, so investors from {abroad} buy more of {home}'s bonds.

slips.S: Investors from {abroad} must buy {cur}s to buy {home}'s bonds, so the demand for the {cur} shifts.

why: Higher real interest rates pull financial capital into {home}; investors buy {cur}s to buy its bonds, so the demand for the {cur} shifts right.
The {cur} appreciates, so {home}'s net exports fall.

scenarios.title: Residents buy more imports
scenarios.cause: Residents of {home} buy more goods made in {abroad}.

slips.D: To buy {abroad}'s goods, {home}'s residents trade their {cur}s for {other}s: they supply {cur}s. Demand for the {cur} comes from abroad.

why: To pay for imports, {home}'s residents sell {cur}s for {other}s: the supply of the {cur} shifts right.
The {cur} depreciates.

scenarios.title: Residents buy foreign assets
scenarios.cause: Investors in {home} buy more stocks and bonds in {abroad}.

slips.D: {home}'s investors sell {cur}s to get the {other}s they need abroad, so the supply of the {cur} shifts.

why: Buying assets in {abroad} takes {other}s, so {home}'s investors supply {cur}s: supply shifts right.
The {cur} depreciates.

scenarios.title: Incomes rise here
scenarios.cause: Incomes in {home} rise, so its residents buy more imports.
scenarios.because: more imports as incomes in {home} rise

slips.D: Higher incomes in {home} raise its imports, so its residents supply more {cur}s. Demand for the {cur} depends on what {abroad} buys.

why: Higher domestic income raises imports: {home}'s residents supply more {cur}s, so supply shifts right.
The {cur} depreciates.

scenarios.title: Incomes rise abroad
scenarios.cause: Incomes in {abroad} rise, so its residents buy more goods from {home}.
why: Richer buyers in {abroad} buy more of {home}'s exports, so they demand more {cur}s: demand shifts right.
The {cur} appreciates.
